content:
To get the most from a rheumatology appointment later in life, write down your two or three most important concerns, bring an up-to-date list of all your medicines (including ones you buy yourself), and note how your joints, morning stiffness, fatigue, falls and everyday tasks have been since your last visit. Bring someone with you if that helps, and tell the clinic beforehand about any hearing, sight, memory or mobility needs. Ask what your treatment target is, which blood tests you need and where they can be done, and how to contact the team if you flare between appointments: NICE says everyone with RA should have rapid access to specialist care for flares. Before you leave, check you understand the plan, and never stop or change a medicine yourself without talking to the team.

This guide helps you prepare for a rheumatology appointment, whether it is your first visit, a follow-up or your annual review, so that a short appointment covers what matters most to you. For what is measured at check-ups, see RA monitoring in later life. If you were diagnosed recently, also read the first months after an RA diagnosis.

In the week before

Appointments can feel rushed, and it is easy to forget things once you are in the room. A little preparation helps:

  • Your top two or three concerns, written down in order of importance
  • A medicines list: everything you take, including dose times, anything you buy from a pharmacy or shop, herbal remedies and creams. Note any side effects and any doses you have missed
  • Symptom notes since your last visit: which joints have been swollen or painful, how long morning stiffness lasts, flares and how long they lasted, fatigue, sleep and mood
  • What you can and cannot do now: for example dressing, opening jars, stairs, walking to the shop, getting out of a chair. These everyday examples tell the team a lot
  • Falls or near-falls, and any new health problems, hospital stays or new medicines from other doctors
  • Your own goals: what you would most like to be able to do again

NRAS, the national RA charity, has free resources on getting the best out of a rheumatology consultation.

Tell the clinic about your needs beforehand

Ring the number on your appointment letter if you have hearing or sight loss, memory problems, need an interpreter, use a wheelchair or walking aid, or find long waits on hard chairs very painful. Ask whether the appointment is face to face, by phone or by video, and prepare the same way for all three.

Getting there

If travel is hard, ask early about NHS non-emergency patient transport or help with travel costs. See getting to appointments and blood tests when travel is hard. Allow extra time, take your medicines with you, and bring a drink and a snack in case of a long wait.

Bring someone with you

A family member, friend or carer can help you remember what was said, take notes and ask the questions you forget. Agree beforehand what you want them to do, and that you will do the talking unless you ask for help.

Questions worth asking

  • Is my arthritis under control? What is my treatment target?
  • What are the benefits and risks of my treatment, and are there other options?
  • Which blood tests do I need, how often, and can they be done nearer home?
  • What should I do if I flare between appointments? What is the advice line number and when is it open?
  • What should I do if I get an infection or feel unwell while on my medicines?
  • Could any of my medicines be adding to dizziness, tiredness or falls?
  • Can I see a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or podiatrist?
  • Are my bones, heart and mood being checked as part of my review?
  • When will I be seen next, and who books it?

What NICE says your care should include

NICE's guideline on rheumatoid arthritis in adults says people with RA should:

  • have treatment risks and benefits explained in ways they can understand, be able to discuss and agree all aspects of their care, and have their decisions respected
  • be offered spoken and written information about RA and its management
  • have a named member of the team (for example a specialist nurse) who co-ordinates their care
  • have access to specialist physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and to a podiatrist if they have foot problems
  • have rapid access to specialist care for flares, information about how to get it, and ongoing drug monitoring
  • be offered an annual review, which checks disease activity and everyday function, looks for other conditions such as high blood pressure, heart disease, osteoporosis and depression, and considers how the disease is affecting their life

Services are organised differently in different places, but these points are a useful checklist for your own care.

Before you leave the room

  • Repeat the plan back in your own words: "So I am going to... and the next blood test is..."
  • Ask for anything important to be written down, including any changes to your medicines
  • Check how you will hear about results and your next appointment
  • Ask for a copy of the clinic letter if you do not usually get one

After the appointment

Write down what you remember as soon as you can. When the clinic letter arrives, check it matches what you understood, and ask your GP or the rheumatology nurse if anything is unclear. You may be able to see letters and test results in the NHS App. If you have a problem with your care that you cannot sort out with the team, the hospital's Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) in England can help.

Some teams use "patient-initiated follow-up", where you ask for an appointment when you need one rather than being given a fixed date. If you are offered this, make sure you know exactly how and when to get in touch.

For family and carers

If you attend with someone, help them prepare their list, but let them lead the conversation as much as they want to. If the person has memory problems, ask the team how you can be kept informed with their agreement. If the hospital day itself is exhausting, see hospital appointment days.

Do not wait for your next appointment if

  • a joint suddenly becomes hot, very swollen and painful and you feel feverish or unwell: get same-day advice from your rheumatology advice line, GP or NHS 111, because a joint infection is an emergency
  • you get new tingling or numbness, weakness in your arms or legs, or new unsteadiness, especially with neck pain: contact your team or GP urgently
  • you have a high temperature or signs of infection while on medicines that affect the immune system: contact your team or NHS 111
  • you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke: call 999

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist, rheumatology nurse or rheumatologist, and never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.
